verdict.rationale: The whole question rides on one verb. The verb 'to empty' (kenoo, G2758) occurs five times in the canon, and in the four uses outside Philippians 2:7 it always means to make void, render of no effect, or nullify something abstract (Romans 4:14 faith made void, 1 Corinthians 1:17 the cross emptied of power, 1 Corinthians 9:15 a boast made void, 2 Corinthians 9:3 a boast made void). It is never used in the New Testament for pouring out a physical substance. So in Philippians 2:7 'he emptied' (ekenosen, a completed past action in the active voice) is metaphorical, and it takes 'himself' (heauton, the reflexive accusative, the 'him-as-direct-object' form) as its direct object, not a list of divine attributes. The two participles that follow tell HOW he emptied himself: 'having taken' (labon) 'the form of a servant' (morphen doulou), and 'having come to be in human likeness' (en homoiomati anthropon genomenos). Both are participles of addition, not subtraction. Colossians 2:9 then says with a present indicative (an ongoing, simple statement of fact) 'dwells' (katoikei) that 'the whole fullness of deity' (pan to pleroma tes theotetos) dwells in him bodily, and Hebrews 1:3 names the incarnate Son 'radiance of the glory' (apaugasma tes doxes) who is 'sustaining all things' (pheron ta panta, present active participle, ongoing action). The lexical pattern is dense and pan-canonical (spread across the whole Bible), but the verdict honestly rests on construing one metaphorical verb by its own canon usage rather than on a literal sense the word does not carry.

scripture.reasoning: Christ 'existing in the form of God' (en morphe theou hyparchon), where 'existing' (hyparchon) is a present active participle (durative, an ongoing or settled subsisting), did not regard 'the being equal with God' (to einai isa theo) as 'something to be grasped' (harpagmon). The noun 'thing-to-be-seized' (harpagmos) is a true hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible, Philippians 2:6 only), glossed 'something to be grasped', so its precise nuance cannot be triangulated from other canon uses. The adjective 'equal' (isos) is stable across its 8 uses as 'equal', and at John 5:18 the same phrase 'making himself equal with God' (ison heauton poion to theo) describes the recognized claim of equality with God. 'Form of God' (morphe theou) and the 'to be equal with God' (to einai isa theo) clause name the actual prior condition of deity that the passage presupposes He continues to possess.

'He emptied' (ekenosen) is morphologically aorist active indicative third singular (a completed past action, in the active voice, simply stated, with 'he' as subject), and it takes 'himself' (heauton, reflexive accusative, the 'him-as-direct-object' form) as its explicit object. No genitive ('from-X' form) or accusative ('direct-object' form) of attributes is supplied as the content of the emptying. The two adverbial participles that immediately specify the act are 'having taken' (labon, aorist active, completed past action) 'form of a servant' (morphen doulou) and 'having come to be in the likeness of men' (en homoiomati anthropon genomenos, aorist, completed past action). Both are verbs of addition. The lexicon classes this very clause under the metaphorical sense 'make empty', alongside 'make void' or 'of no effect', not under the literal 'pour out a substance' sense. So the emptying is impoverishment by assuming servant form and human likeness, not divestment of deity.

'All the fullness of the deity dwells in him bodily' (Pan to pleroma tes theotetos katoikei en auto somatikos). The verb 'dwells' (katoikei) is present active indicative (durative, ongoing settled dwelling, simply stated as fact), 'all the fullness' (pan to pleroma) is universal quantifying (the whole fullness), 'of deity' (theotetos) is the abstract noun for deity itself and is a hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible, Colossians 2:9 only, glossed 'Deity'), distinct from the quality noun 'divinity' (theiotes), and 'bodily' (somatikos, adverb) locates this fullness in the incarnate body. The present tense and the abstract essence noun together exclude any present subtraction of divine essence or attributes from the incarnate Christ.

'The Word became flesh' (Ho logos sarx egeneto) uses 'became' (egeneto, aorist of 'to become', ginomai, a completed past action) for the assumption of flesh, not an exchange or loss of natures. The clause that immediately follows, 'we beheld his glory' (etheasametha ten doxan autou, aorist of 'to behold', theaomai, completed past action), reports that eyewitnesses saw his glory as 'of an only-begotten from a father' (monogenous para patros, where monogenes means one-of-a-kind) during the incarnation. Glory of the only-begotten (monogenes, one-of-a-kind) was visible in the enfleshed 'Word' (Logos), not surrendered.

The Son is 'radiance of the glory' (apaugasma tes doxes, where 'radiance' (apaugasma) is a hapax, a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) and 'exact impress of his very being' (charakter tes hypostaseos autou), and the participle 'sustaining all things by the word of his power' (pheron ta panta to rhemati tes dynameos autou) is present active (an ongoing action, in the active voice). The same subject who, having made 'cleansing of sins' (katharismon ton hamartion), sat down, is the one presently sustaining the cosmos. Active omnipotence is therefore predicated of the incarnate Son, which a present surrender of divine power would contradict.

complicating_texts.resolution: The cited anchor itself is the strongest kenotic prooftext if 'he emptied' (ekenosen) is read absolutely as 'poured out his deity'. The grammar refuses that reading. The verb is transitive with 'himself' (heauton) as its accusative ('direct-object' form) object, and the manner participles 'having taken' (labon) and 'having come to be' (genomenos) supply addition of servant form and human likeness as the content of the act. No word for any divine attribute is named as what was emptied out. The canon usage of 'to empty' (kenoo, four other times meaning 'make void' or 'of no effect') confirms the metaphorical sense over a literal divestment.

'No one knows, not even the Son' (Oudeis oiden, oude ho huios) the day or hour. This is predicated of the Son in his incarnate economic state and reports a limitation in the mode of human knowing, not surrender of an essential divine attribute. The same Gospel tradition presents the incarnate Jesus knowing all things: John 2:24-25 (he knew all men, 'to know all' (ginoskein pantas), and needed no witness about man), John 16:30 ('you know all things', oidas panta), and John 21:17 ('you know all things', panta su oidas). The lexical pattern of Philippians 2:7 (reflexive emptying by addition) and Colossians 2:9 (present indwelling of 'all the fullness of the deity' (pan to pleroma tes theotetos)) governs the synthesis.

'The Son can do nothing of himself' (Ou dynatai ho huios poiein aph heautou ouden) but only what he sees the Father doing. The clause states relational dependence within the Trinity, not a confession that omnipotence was relinquished. It pairs with John 5:21 in the same discourse where the Son 'gives life to whom he wills' (hous thelei zoopoiei), an act predicated of God.

'Jesus advanced in wisdom and stature' (Iesous proekopten sophia kai helikia, with 'advanced' (prokopto) imperfect, ongoing or repeated past action, intransitive growth). This describes development within the true human nature of the incarnate Son. It is not a statement that divine omniscience was divested, since the same person elsewhere is shown knowing the hearts of all (John 2:24-25).

variant_units_examined.note: The base text reads 'through himself' (di heautou) for the means by which the Son made 'cleansing' (katharismon), and witnesses vary toward 'through him' (di autou). Both readings preserve 'radiance' (apaugasma), 'exact impress of his very being' (charakter tes hypostaseos), and the present participle 'sustaining all things' (pheron ta panta), so the deity-retention witness is untouched. Not in the ingested ECM (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) window, standard apparatus only.

Witnesses vary between 'of men' (anthropon, plural) and 'of a man' (anthropou, singular) after 'in the likeness' (homoiomati). The variant shifts the scope of the human likeness but leaves the reflexive object 'himself' (heauton), the verb 'he emptied' (ekenosen), and the manner participles 'having taken' (labon) and 'having come to be' (genomenos) unchanged. Not in the ingested ECM (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) window, standard apparatus only.

The variant survey above relies on the standard printed apparatus, and neither variant touches the syntax that decides the verdict.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads 'he emptied' (ekenosen) reflexively (with 'himself' (heauton) as the object), treats 'having taken' (labon) and 'having come to be' (genomenos) as manner participles of addition, and harmonizes Philippians 2:6-7 with the present indicative (ongoing, simple statement of fact) 'all the fullness of the deity dwells' (pan to pleroma tes theotetos katoikei) of Colossians 2:9 and the present participle 'sustaining all things' (pheron ta panta) of Hebrews 1:3. The incarnation is assumption of a true human nature with no subtraction from deity. This reading aligns with the canon usage of 'to empty' (kenoo) as metaphorical 'make void' rather than literal 'pour out'.

Reads 'he emptied' (ekenosen) as actual divestment, supplying an implied object of divine attributes (omniscience, omnipotence, omnipresence) that the Son laid aside during the incarnation, and appeals to texts like Mark 13:32 (the Son not knowing the day or hour) as evidence of a real surrender. Stated at its strongest, this lens takes 'emptied' as the natural force of the verb and reads the participles as describing the resulting state of servanthood. The lexical objections it must answer are that Philippians 2:7 supplies 'himself' (heauton) as the explicit object and names no attribute as content, that 'to empty' (kenoo) elsewhere means 'make void' of an abstraction rather than 'pour out' a substance, and that Colossians 2:9 and Hebrews 1:3 predicate present full deity and active sustaining of the incarnate Son.

Reads 'he emptied' (ekenosen) as the Son voluntarily veiling or not independently exercising certain divine prerogatives in the incarnate state, rather than ontologically losing them. This is grammatically compatible with the reflexive 'himself' (heauton), with the manner participles, and with the present tense retention texts, and it converges with the verdict that no attribute of deity is surrendered. It treats texts like John 5:19 and Mark 13:32 as descriptions of the incarnate mode of operating within a true human nature.

hermeneutics.notes: The three lenses construe the same Greek differently, and the divergence is genuinely lexical. It turns on whether 'he emptied' (ekenosen) is read absolutely with an implied object of attributes or transitively with 'himself' (heauton) and the manner participles. The queried canon usage of 'to empty' (kenoo, in Romans 4:14, 1 Corinthians 1:17, 1 Corinthians 9:15, 2 Corinthians 9:3 all meaning 'make void' or 'of no effect', never 'pour out a substance') plus the present tense indwelling of Colossians 2:9 and sustaining of Hebrews 1:3 weigh toward the retention readings, but the surrender reading is a coherent construal of an ambiguous absolute verb and is represented here at its strongest.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: In Philippians 2:6-7, Colossians 2:9, John 1:14, and Hebrews 1:3, does the lexical pattern indicate that in the incarnation the Son surrendered or gave up divine attributes proper to his deity, retained them in full, or voluntarily restrained their exercise?
stem_audit.notes: The proposition is a denial stem. It encodes its own conclusion by predicating that Christ took a human nature without surrendering divine attributes, which is the denial of kenoticism rather than an open question. The verdict was still derived on the original stem from the lexical data. The neutralized form keeps the same anchors and lemmas in view but reframes the issue as an open inquiry across the surrender, full-retention, and voluntary-non-use options so the verdict is not smuggled by the wording.

lay_summary: Everything here hangs on one Greek verb. Philippians 2:7 says the Son emptied himself, and the word for 'emptied' is 'to empty' (kenoo). That verb appears five times in the New Testament. In the other four places it never means to pour out a physical substance. It means to make void, to nullify, to render of no effect: faith made void in Romans 4:14, the cross emptied of its power in 1 Corinthians 1:17, a boast made void in 1 Corinthians 9:15 and 2 Corinthians 9:3. So in Philippians 2:7 the word is a metaphor, made himself nothing, not a literal pouring away of his deity. The grammar settles what the emptying was. The verb takes 'himself' (heauton) as its object, not a list of divine attributes, and the two phrases that follow say how he emptied himself: by 'taking' (labon) 'the form of a servant' (morphen doulou) and by 'coming to be' (genomenos) in 'the likeness' (homoiomati) of human beings. That is emptying by addition, by taking on, not by subtracting anything he already had. Two more passages confirm it. Colossians 2:9 says 'the whole fullness of deity' (pan to pleroma tes theotetos) 'dwells' (katoikei) in him bodily, and the verb 'dwells' is present tense, an ongoing settled state, with deity (theotes) named as the very essence, not just qualities. Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son 'the radiance of the glory' (apaugasma tes doxes) and says he is 'sustaining all things' (pheron ta panta) by his powerful word, present tense, during the incarnation, which is omnipotence still at work. Texts read the other way, like Mark 13:32 where the Son does not know the day or hour, John 5:19 where he does nothing of himself, and Luke 2:52 where he grew in wisdom, all describe the incarnate Son living and acting through a real human nature. They never say a divine attribute was given up. Honesty requires noting that the whole case rests on reading one metaphorical verb by its own usage, so the divergence among readers is genuinely about that single word, but the canon pattern of the words favors retention of the divine attributes during the incarnation.
